title: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
summary: How a next-token predictor becomes an assistant: pretraining on trillions of tokens, supervised fine-tuning with a masked loss, reward models from human rankings, and RL with a KL penalty.
outcomes: Explain why a pretrained base model is not an assistant and what each of pretraining, SFT and RLHF adds
Compute next-token cross-entropy for a short sequence and estimate pretraining compute with C of about 6ND
Implement SFT loss masking and explain why prompt tokens are excluded but the end-of-turn token is not
Compute Bradley-Terry reward model probabilities and losses from a human ranking
Explain how the KL penalty, beta and reward over-optimization interact in PPO-based RLHF and its alternatives

lessons.title: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe

blocks.md: The GPT you built is trained to do one thing: predict the next token of text. Train that model on a large slice of the internet and you get a **base model** (also called a pretrained model). It knows a great deal about language, facts and code, but it was never asked to *help* anyone. Given a question, it produces whatever text is most likely to come next in a document, which might be an answer, or might be more questions in the same style.

The InstructGPT paper (Ouyang et al., 2022) put the gap plainly: predicting the next token on a webpage is a different objective from "follow the user's instructions helpfully and safely", so the language modeling objective is **misaligned** with what users want. The fix it popularized is a three-stage recipe that most chat models still follow in some form:

1. **Pretraining**: next-token prediction on hundreds of billions to trillions of tokens of raw text.
2. **Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)**: the same loss, but on a small set of prompts paired with answers written by people.
3. **RLHF** (reinforcement learning from human feedback): people compare model answers, a **reward model** learns to predict their preferences, and reinforcement learning pushes the model toward answers the reward model scores highly.

scenes.caption: Stage 1: pretraining. GPT-3 was trained on 300 billion tokens of mostly web text. The result predicts text well but does not reliably follow instructions.
Stage 2: SFT. Labelers wrote good answers for about 13k prompts, and the base model is fine-tuned on them with the ordinary next-token loss.
Stage 3a: reward model. Labelers rank several model answers per prompt (about 33k prompts). A 6B model, started from an SFT model, learns to give preferred answers a higher score.
Stage 3b: RL. The SFT model becomes a policy that writes answers to about 31k prompts; the reward model scores them and PPO updates the policy toward higher scores.

blocks.md: A useful mental model: pretraining puts the knowledge and skills into the weights; SFT teaches the *format* and role of an assistant; RLHF sharpens the choice among answers the model can already produce, using a signal ("which of these is better?") that is much cheaper to collect than writing perfect answers.

The later stages are tiny next to pretraining. InstructGPT reports that training the 175B SFT model took 4.9 petaflop/s-days and the 175B PPO-ptx model took 60, compared with 3,640 petaflop/s-days to pretrain GPT-3. A petaflop/s-day is $10^{15}$ operations per second sustained for a day, about $8.64 \times 10^{19}$ operations.

scenes.caption: Pretraining GPT-3 175B: 3,640 petaflop/s-days. Everything else is measured against this.
SFT adds 4.9 petaflop/s-days (about 0.13 percent of pretraining) and PPO-ptx adds 60 (about 1.6 percent). The bars are barely visible: alignment is cheap in compute, expensive in human labeling.

blocks.md: Same network, three different training signals: raw text (what comes next?), demonstrations (what would a good assistant write?), and comparisons (which of these two answers is better?). Each stage starts from the weights of the previous one.

The payoff was large. In InstructGPT's human evaluations on their API prompt distribution, outputs from the **1.3B** InstructGPT model were preferred to outputs from the **175B** GPT-3, a model over 100 times larger. The paper also found an **alignment tax**: RLHF lowered scores on some public benchmarks such as SQuAD and DROP, which they reduced by mixing pretraining updates into RL (the "ptx" in PPO-ptx).

blocks.question: A base model is given the prompt "Write a haiku about rain." Why might it fail to write a haiku?
options: Its weights contain no knowledge of poetry, which only SFT adds
It continues the text as a plausible document, which may be more instructions or a list of prompts rather than an answer
Base models cannot generate text without a reward model
The prompt is too short for the attention mechanism
blocks.explain: Pretraining optimizes next-token likelihood on documents. A line like this often appears in lists of writing prompts, so continuing with more prompts is a likely continuation. The knowledge of haiku is already in the base model; SFT and RLHF teach it to respond as an assistant.

blocks.question: Roughly what fraction of GPT-3's pretraining compute did the 175B InstructGPT PPO-ptx run use?
options: About 50 percent
About 16 percent
About 1.6 percent
About 0.01 percent
blocks.explain: 60 / 3,640 is about 0.0165, so about 1.6 percent. The scarce input for alignment is human data (demonstrations and comparisons), not compute.

lessons.title: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens

blocks.md: Pretraining is the training loop from your GPT, scaled up. Take a long document, split it into tokens, and at every position ask the model for a probability distribution over the whole vocabulary for the *next* token. The loss at that position is the **cross-entropy**: the negative log of the probability the model gave to the token that actually came next.

blocks.caption: Average next-token cross-entropy over T predictions. Every position in every document is a training example, so no labels are needed.

blocks.md: Let us run it on a toy. The vocabulary has five words: `the`, `cat`, `sat`, `on`, `mat`. The document is "the cat sat on the". The inputs are the first four tokens, and the targets are the same tokens shifted left by one. We made up the model's logits; the probabilities and losses below are computed from them with a softmax.

blocks.title: One document becomes four training examples

scenes.caption: The model reads the input tokens. Because of the causal mask, position t only sees tokens 0 to t, so all four predictions are computed in one forward pass.
Targets are the inputs shifted left by one. Position 0 ("the") must predict "cat", position 2 ("sat") must predict "on".
Softmax over the five logits gives the probability assigned to each correct next token. "cat sat" is easy (0.702); "sat on" is hardest (0.336).
Loss per position is -ln p. The low-probability guess costs the most (1.090). The mean over 4 positions is 0.703, a perplexity of exp(0.703), about 2.02.

blocks.prompt: The gradient of cross-entropy with respect to the logits is $p - \text{onehot}(\text{target})$. At the "sat" position the target is "on". If we take one gradient step on these logits, what happens to the probabilities of the four *wrong* words?
blocks.reveal: They all go down, and the correct word goes up. The gradient is positive for every wrong word (its probability $p_k$) and negative for the target ($p_{on} - 1 = -0.664$), so subtracting it raises the target logit and lowers the others in proportion to how much probability they stole. The loss at that position drops from 1.090 to 0.618 after one step with learning rate 1.

blocks.title: One gradient step at the "sat" position

scenes.caption: Before: the model spreads probability, giving the target "on" only 0.336 (loss 1.090).
After one step with learning rate 1: "on" rises to 0.539 (loss 0.618). Simplified: we nudged the 5 logits directly; a real model changes its weights, which moves logits at many positions at once.
With learning rate 2 instead: "on" reaches 0.729 (loss 0.316). Larger steps fit this example faster but, on real data, overshoot and destabilize training.

blocks.md: Scale changes the engineering, not the objective. GPT-3 trained every model size on **300 billion tokens**. Llama 3's flagship model has 405B parameters and was trained on **15.6 trillion tokens**. Data is a weighted mix, not one pile: GPT-3 drew 60 percent of examples from filtered Common Crawl, 22 percent from WebText2, 8 percent each from two book corpora and 3 percent from Wikipedia, deliberately not in proportion to dataset size.

blocks.title: GPT-3's pretraining mix: size vs sampling weight

scenes.caption: Dataset sizes in billions of tokens: Common Crawl dwarfs everything else (410B of the 499B).
Epochs seen during the 300B-token run. Higher-quality sets were upsampled: Wikipedia was seen 3.4 times and WebText2 2.9 times, while Common Crawl was seen only 0.44 times.

blocks.md: How much compute does that take? Kaplan et al. (2020) estimate training compute as about $6N$ floating point operations per token for a model with $N$ parameters: roughly $2N$ for the forward pass and twice that for the backward pass. Multiply by the number of training tokens $D$.

blocks.caption: GPT-3 175B. The paper's table lists 3.14e23 FLOPs (3,640 petaflop/s-days). For Llama 3 405B on 15.6T tokens the same rule gives about 3.8e25, matching the reported 3.8 x 10^25.

blocks.md: A low pretraining loss does not mean a helpful model. The loss rewards matching the *distribution* of internet text, including its errors, rudeness and rambling. That is exactly why the later stages exist.
How to split a fixed compute budget between parameters N and tokens D is the subject of the Scaling laws course; here just remember that $C \approx 6ND$ ties the two together.

blocks.question: A model with a 50,000-token vocabulary predicts the uniform distribution at every position. What is its average cross-entropy loss?
options: 0 nats, because it never assigns zero probability
About 10.8 nats, which is ln(50,000)
About 0.69 nats, which is ln(2)
50,000 nats
blocks.explain: Uniform means p(target) = 1/50,000 everywhere, so the loss is -ln(1/50,000) = ln(50,000), about 10.82 nats. Real training starts near this value and falls as the model learns.

blocks.question: Using C of about 6ND, a 7B-parameter model trained on 2 trillion tokens needs roughly how many FLOPs?
blocks.explain: 6 x 7e9 x 2e12 = 8.4e22. The rule ignores attention's context-length term, which Kaplan et al. note is small when the model width is large relative to the context.

lessons.title: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt

blocks.md: **Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)**, also called instruction tuning, continues training the base model on examples of the behavior you want: a prompt, followed by an ideal response. The loss is the same next-token cross-entropy as pretraining. What changes is the data and which tokens count.

Each example is rendered with a **chat template**: special tokens that mark who is speaking, such as a user header, the user's text, an assistant header, the answer, and an end-of-turn token. At inference time the serving system writes the user header, the user's text and the assistant header, and the model continues from there. SFT teaches the model what belongs after the assistant header and, importantly, when to stop.

blocks.title: Loss masking on one SFT example

scenes.caption: One SFT example: 6 template and prompt tokens, then a 4-token answer that ends in an end-of-sequence token.
Every token after the first is a prediction target. Illustrative per-token losses: the prompt is hard to predict (the user could ask anything), the answer is easier.
Averaging all 9 gives 2.02, and the 5 prompt tokens make up 78 percent of the summed loss. Training on that would mostly teach the model to imitate users.
Mask the prompt: only the 4 answer targets count, mean loss 1.00. The model still reads the prompt as context; it just is not graded on predicting it.

blocks.md: Llama 2 describes exactly this: "we zero-out the loss on tokens from the user prompt, so as a result, we backpropagate only on answer tokens." It also concatenates all the prompts and answers to fill each 4,096-token sequence, with a special token separating prompt and answer segments, so no compute is wasted on padding. In PyTorch the usual trick is to set masked label positions to `-100`, the default `ignore_index` of the cross-entropy loss.

blocks.title: Masked SFT loss in PyTorch
blocks.code:
import torch.nn.functional as F

# input_ids: [B, T]  (6 prompt tokens, then 4 answer tokens)
labels = input_ids.clone()
labels[:, :n_prompt] = -100        # mask template + prompt

logits = model(input_ids)          # [B, T, V]
shift_logits = logits[:, :-1]      # position t predicts t+1
shift_labels = labels[:, 1:]

loss = F.cross_entropy(
    shift_logits.reshape(-1, V),
    shift_labels.reshape(-1),
    ignore_index=-100,             # skip masked targets
)

scenes.caption: Copy the token ids to use as labels.
Overwrite the first n_prompt = 6 labels with -100, so they will be ignored.
One forward pass over all 10 tokens; the model still attends to the prompt.
Shift so that position t is scored on token t+1: 9 predictions remain.
Cross-entropy averages only over the 4 non-ignored targets. With the earlier numbers this is 1.00, not 2.02.

blocks.md: SFT data is small and curated. InstructGPT used about 13k prompts with labeler-written answers and trained for 16 epochs; the SFT models overfit on validation loss after one epoch, yet more epochs still improved reward model scores and human preference. Llama 2 stopped after **27,540** high-quality annotations, finding that a few tens of thousands of clean examples beat millions of noisier third-party ones.

LIMA (Zhou et al., 2023) pushed this further: fine-tuning a 65B LLaMa model on only **1,000** carefully chosen examples (about 750,000 tokens) produced a strong assistant. The authors state the **Superficial Alignment Hypothesis**: almost all knowledge is learned in pretraining, and alignment mostly teaches the style and format to use when talking to users.

SFT does not add much new knowledge. If the base model does not know a fact, a demonstration that states it mostly teaches the model to answer confidently in that style, which can increase made-up answers on other questions ([Gekhman et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05904)).
SFT = pretraining loss + chat template + loss only on response tokens (including the end-of-turn token) + a small, high-quality dataset.

blocks.question: A team fine-tunes on chat data but forgets to mask the prompt. What is the most likely symptom?
options: Training crashes because labels and logits have different lengths
The model learns to write user-style questions and the loss is dominated by hard-to-predict prompt tokens
The model forgets the chat template entirely
Nothing changes, because the prompt loss gradient is always zero
blocks.explain: Without the mask the model is also trained to predict user text, which is high-entropy and dominates the average (78 percent of the summed loss in our example). Capacity and gradient go into imitating users instead of answering them.

blocks.question: Why must the end-of-sequence token after the answer be included in the trained targets?
options: It carries the reward signal for RLHF
Otherwise the model never learns when to stop and keeps generating
It is required by the softmax
It prevents the prompt from being masked
blocks.explain: Stopping is a learned prediction like any other. If the end token is masked, the model never sees a gradient for ending its turn and tends to run on, for example by writing the next user turn itself.

lessons.title: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score

blocks.md: Writing a perfect answer is slow; saying which of two answers is better is fast and more consistent across people. RLHF exploits this. A **reward model** $r_\theta(x, y)$ reads a prompt $x$ and a response $y$ and outputs one number. InstructGPT builds it from an SFT model by removing the final unembedding layer (the projection to vocabulary logits) and adding a head that outputs a scalar.

Training uses the **Bradley-Terry** model of comparisons: the probability that a person prefers response $y_w$ (winner) over $y_l$ (loser) is the sigmoid of the reward difference. The loss is the negative log of that probability, averaged over human comparisons. This is the loss in InstructGPT (Equation 1) and Llama 2.

blocks.caption: sigma(z) = 1 / (1 + e^{-z}). Only the difference of rewards matters, so the reward scale is anchored only by the data.

blocks.md: InstructGPT showed labelers between $K=4$ and $K=9$ responses per prompt and asked for a full ranking. A ranking of $K$ items implies $\binom{K}{2}$ pairs: 6 pairs for $K=4$, 36 for $K=9$. Because those pairs share responses, InstructGPT puts all pairs from one prompt in the same batch element; shuffling them as independent examples made the reward model overfit after one pass.

Worked example. A labeler ranks four responses A > B > C > D. Before training, every reward is 0, every pairwise probability is 0.5 and every pair costs $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$. After training, suppose the rewards are A = 1.2, B = 0.5, C = 0.1, D = -0.8.

blocks.title: P(row is preferred over column) from rewards

scenes.caption: Untrained: all rewards equal, so every comparison is a coin flip (0.5). Mean loss over the 6 ranked pairs is ln 2, about 0.693.
Trained rewards A=1.2, B=0.5, C=0.1, D=-0.8. The upper triangle holds the 6 labeled pairs; each is sigma of the reward gap.
Largest gap: A vs D (2.0) gives 0.88 and loss 0.127. Smallest: B vs C (0.4) gives 0.60 and loss 0.513, the pair the model is least sure about. Mean loss falls to 0.319.
Read across a row to see how likely that response is to beat each other one. The matrix is antisymmetric around 0.5: P(B over A) = 1 - P(A over B) = 0.33.

blocks.prompt: Add 5 to every reward (A = 6.2, B = 5.5, C = 5.1, D = 4.2). What happens to the loss?
blocks.reveal: Nothing. Every pairwise probability depends only on differences, so A vs B is still $\sigma(0.7) = 0.668$ and the loss is unchanged. The reward model's absolute level is arbitrary, which is why InstructGPT adds a bias so that labeler demonstrations score 0 on average before RL.

scenes.caption: With m = 0 this is the InstructGPT loss. A wrongly ordered pair (negative gap) is punished almost linearly; a confidently correct pair costs almost nothing.

Llama 2 subtracts a margin m that grows with how strongly the annotator preferred the winner. With m = 3 (the 'significantly better' value in its larger margin variant) the loss stays high until the gap exceeds 3.

blocks.md: A reward model is a learned approximation, not ground truth. Stiennon et al. found their summarization reward model preferred longer summaries, and it can be confidently wrong on responses unlike its training data. The next lesson shows what happens when RL optimizes hard against such a model.
The reward model learns only from differences. Its job is to rank responses to the same prompt, and its output is a log-odds score: a gap of 1 means about 73 percent preference.

blocks.question: A labeler ranks K = 6 responses. How many pairwise comparisons does that give, and how many gradient terms does each single response appear in?
options: 6 pairs; each response appears in 1
15 pairs; each response appears in 5
30 pairs; each response appears in 10
36 pairs; each response appears in 6
blocks.explain: C(6,2) = 15 pairs, and each response is compared with the other K - 1 = 5. That correlation is why InstructGPT batches all pairs from one prompt together instead of shuffling them.

blocks.question: Rewards are A = 2.0 and B = 1.0, and the human preferred B. What is the loss on this pair?
blocks.explain: The winner is B, so the gap is 1.0 - 2.0 = -1. Loss = -ln sigma(-1) = ln(1 + e) = 1.313. A wrongly ordered pair costs much more than ln 2.

lessons.title: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model

blocks.md: Now we treat the language model as a **policy** $\pi_\phi(y \mid x)$: given a prompt, it samples a response. InstructGPT frames this as a **bandit** environment: a prompt arrives, the policy writes a whole response, the reward model scores it once, and the episode ends. The goal is to raise expected reward.

Maximizing the reward model alone fails quickly: the policy drifts to strange text where the reward model was never trained and is easy to fool. So the reward is penalized by how far the policy has moved from the SFT model. This is the objective from Stiennon et al. (2020), used by InstructGPT, with $\beta = 0.02$ in InstructGPT's runs.

blocks.caption: The expected value of the log ratio is the KL divergence from the SFT model. InstructGPT applies the penalty per token and also adds gamma times the pretraining log-likelihood (PPO-ptx).

scenes.caption: Rollout: the policy (initialized from the SFT model) samples a response for each prompt at temperature 1. InstructGPT used batches of 512 episodes.
Scoring: the frozen reward model gives one scalar per response, and the frozen SFT model gives log-probabilities for every token so the KL penalty can be computed.
A value model, initialized from the reward model, predicts the expected return at each token. Subtracting it gives advantages: was this token better or worse than expected?

PPO updates the policy on these samples with a clipped objective, so it gains nothing from moving any token's probability ratio more than 20 percent, then the loop repeats. Four models are in play: two trained, two frozen.

blocks.md: The KL penalty is paid token by token. For each response token, compute the log-probability under the policy and under the SFT model; their difference is that token's contribution. The reward model's score is added at the final token. Here is a 4-token response with reward model score 1.5.

blocks.title: Per-token KL penalty on one response

scenes.caption: Log-probabilities of the 4 sampled tokens under the current policy and the frozen SFT model (illustrative values).
Log ratios: the policy has made tokens 0, 1 and 3 more likely than SFT did (sum 1.3 nats). Token 2 is unchanged.
With beta = 0.02, each token earns -0.02 times its log ratio, and the last token also gets the score 1.5. Total reward 1.5 - 0.026 = 1.474.
With beta = 0.1 the same drift costs five times more: total 1.5 - 0.13 = 1.37. Larger beta keeps the policy closer to SFT.

blocks.md: PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) is the optimizer. Its key idea is a **clipped** objective: with probability ratio $\rho = \pi_{new}/\pi_{old}$ for a token and advantage $A$, it maximizes $\min(\rho A, \operatorname{clip}(\rho, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) A)$. With $\epsilon = 0.2$ (InstructGPT's setting), a token with $A = +1$ whose ratio already reached 1.5 is credited only 1.2, so there is no gradient pushing it further. This lets PPO take several minibatch steps on one batch of samples without the policy running away.

blocks.prompt: Ignore the KL term and suppose the policy could put all its probability on any response it likes. Which response would pure reward maximization pick?
blocks.reveal: The single response with the highest reward model score, with probability 1, whether or not humans actually like it. Pure maximization collapses diversity and finds the reward model's blind spots. The KL term is what keeps the optimum spread over responses the SFT model considered plausible.

blocks.md: RLHF does not maximize reward. It maximizes reward minus beta times the KL from the SFT model, and beta sets how far the model may move to chase the reward model.

blocks.question: During RLHF, the mean reward keeps rising while the KL from the SFT model shoots up and samples start repeating odd phrases. Which change most directly addresses this?
options: Lower beta so the policy can explore more
Raise beta, or stop at an earlier checkpoint
Lower the PPO clip range to 0
Remove the value model
blocks.explain: Rising reward with exploding KL is the signature of the policy exploiting the reward model. A larger beta makes drift more expensive, and earlier checkpoints have less drift. Lowering beta makes it worse; a clip range of 0 stops learning entirely.

blocks.question: Why does InstructGPT keep a frozen copy of the SFT model during RL?
options: To generate the training prompts
To compute log-probabilities for the KL penalty that anchors the policy
To replace the reward model when it is uncertain
To serve as the value function
blocks.explain: The frozen SFT model supplies log pi_SFT for every sampled token, which the per-token KL penalty compares with the policy's log-probabilities. The value function is a separate model initialized from the reward model.

lessons.title: Reward over-optimization, best-of-N and modern recipes

blocks.md: The KL-regularized objective has a closed-form best policy, derived in the DPO paper (Rafailov et al., 2023): reweight the SFT model's probabilities by the exponentiated reward. Small $\beta$ means sharp reweighting; large $\beta$ means staying near SFT. Real PPO only approximates this optimum, but it shows exactly where the tradeoff comes from.

blocks.caption: Z(x) normalizes the distribution over responses. A response gains probability exponentially in its reward, but starts from its SFT probability.

blocks.md: A toy with four possible responses. The SFT model gives them probabilities 0.25, 0.35, 0.30, 0.10. The reward model scores them 1.0, -0.5, 0.3, 1.5. But the reward model is flawed: the **Flattery** response scores highest, while humans actually rate it -0.4 (they rate the other three 1.0, -0.5 and 0.2). We compute $\pi^*$ for several $\beta$ and track the reward model's score and the true quality.

blocks.title: The optimal policy as beta shrinks

scenes.caption: beta = 100: essentially the SFT model. RM score 0.32, true quality 0.10, KL 0.00.
beta = 2: the Wrong answer loses mass first. RM score 0.56, true quality 0.21, KL 0.06. Light optimization genuinely helps.
beta = 1: Helpful leads at 0.39. RM score 0.78, true quality 0.27 near its best, KL 0.23.
beta = 0.5: Flattery overtakes Helpful. RM score keeps rising to 1.10 but true quality has dropped to 0.24 (KL 0.68).
beta = 0.25: Flattery takes 0.73. RM score 1.35, true quality -0.04, worse than the SFT model (KL 1.40).
beta = 0.1: near-total collapse onto the hacked response. RM score 1.49, true quality -0.38. Simplified: real models have astronomically many responses, but the dynamics match.

blocks.title: Proxy reward vs true quality as optimization grows

scenes.caption: Same toy, swept continuously. The proxy reward rises monotonically with optimization, as does the KL from the SFT model.

True quality peaks at 0.28 near 1/beta = 1.3 (KL 0.36), then falls below the starting point. Stiennon et al. saw this with real summaries: past some KL, the reward model became anti-correlated with human preference.

blocks.md: A higher reward model score is not evidence of a better model. Teams track KL and check with fresh human or held-out evaluations, because the proxy keeps climbing after real quality has turned down. This is Goodhart's law applied to learned rewards; the Reward hacking course goes deeper.

**Best-of-N** (rejection sampling) is a simpler way to use a reward model: sample $N$ responses, keep the highest-scoring one. Stiennon et al. give its KL from the base policy as $\log N - (N-1)/N$ nats: about 0.64 for $N=4$, 1.84 for $N=16$ and 3.86 for $N=128$. Llama 2 used rejection sampling fine-tuning (train on the best of $K$ samples, like SFT) for its early RLHF rounds, then applied PPO on top.

**Direct Preference Optimization** (DPO) uses the closed form above in reverse: it rewrites the reward in terms of the policy's own log-probability ratio against the reference model, so the Bradley-Terry loss can be applied to the policy directly. No separate reward model at training time and no sampling loop. Llama 3's post-training ran six rounds of SFT, rejection sampling with a reward model, and DPO, which its authors chose over PPO partly because it needed less compute at scale. DPO and its variants have their own course.

scenes.caption: InstructGPT (2022): one pass of SFT, reward model, then PPO with a KL penalty and pretraining mix.
Llama 2-Chat (2023): SFT, then iterated RLHF versions V1 to V5 with fresh preference data each time: rejection sampling alone until V4, then PPO applied on top of a rejection-sampled checkpoint.
Llama 3 (2024): six rounds, each with a reward model, rejection-sampled SFT data, SFT, then DPO instead of PPO. Simplified: rounds drawn as equal-length blocks.

blocks.md: Whatever the algorithm, the ingredients are the same three: a strong pretrained model, a small set of high-quality demonstrations, and preference data with a mechanism (PPO, rejection sampling or DPO) that moves the model toward preferred answers while staying near a reference.

blocks.question: In the toy, which beta gives the best true quality among the ones shown, and why is the smallest beta not best?
options: beta = 0.1, because it has the highest reward model score
beta = 1, because past it the policy shifts mass to the response the reward model overrates
beta = 100, because any change from SFT hurts
All are equal, because the reward model is unbiased on average
blocks.explain: True quality is 0.27 at beta = 1 versus 0.24 at 0.5 and -0.38 at 0.1. Small beta lets the policy concentrate on Flattery, which the reward model overrates. Some optimization helps: beta = 100 leaves quality at 0.10.

blocks.question: Best-of-N with N = 64 moves the output distribution how far from the base policy, by the analytic formula?
options: About 0.98 nats
About 3.18 nats
About 4.16 nats
About 64 nats
blocks.explain: log 64 - 63/64 = 4.159 - 0.984 = 3.175 nats. KL grows only logarithmically in N, which is why best-of-N is a gentle form of optimization.
